Empirical Research Plan – “Tariff-Uncertainty Shock and the Post-2000 U.S. Manufacturing Decline”

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
1. Identification Strategy
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Method: Difference-in-Differences (DID) with a continuous treatment intensity, complemented by an event-study and a triple-difference (US vs. EU).

Why DID is appropriate:
• The policy shock (PNTR, effective Jan-2002) is sharp and common across the U.S., but industries differ ex-ante in how strongly its removal of tariff-uncertainty matters – the “NTR-gap” (= non-NTR – NTR tariff) provides quasi-random cross-sectional exposure.  
• The same industries in the EU did not experience a policy change, offering a credible benchmark to net out China-related world-wide shocks.  
• The panel structure (industry × year, or plant × year) allows us to compare differential pre/post paths in high- vs. low-gap industries.

Basic estimating equation (industry level):
Y_it = α_i + γ_t + β (Post_t × NTRgap_i) + ε_it                        (1)

Triple-diff:
Y_ict = α_ic + γ_t + δ_c + β (US_c × Post_t × NTRgap_i) + ε_ict   (2)
 i = industry, c = country (US or EU).  

Event-study: replace Post_t × NTRgap_i with Σ_k≠−1 θ_k × 1[τ=k] × NTRgap_i, τ measured in years from 2001 = -1 baseline.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Treatment and Control
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Treatment variable  
• Continuous: NTRgap_i = statutory non-NTR rate – NTR rate for industry i (percent).  
• For some robustness, define HighGap_i = 1[ NTRgap_i ≥ median ].

Control group  
• Industries with low or zero gaps are the within-US counterfactual.  
• EU industries (same 4-digit ISIC) serve as an external counterfactual in the triple-diff.

Treatment timing / event date  
• Oct-2000 (announcement) or Jan-2002 (effective). I will treat 2001 forward as Post=1 and test sensitivity to using 2002.

No RDD – there is no discontinuous cutoff in the running variable.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Key Identifying Assumptions
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
A1. Parallel trends: In the absence of PNTR, high-gap and low-gap (and US vs. EU) industries would have evolved similarly.  
Plausibility: The gap is based on Smoot-Hawley schedules set in 1930—unlikely to be correlated with 1990s trend differences; we will document pre-trends graphically.

A2. No differential contemporaneous shocks correlated with NTRgap.  
Plausibility: Need to rule out China’s own productivity or EU policy shifts that load on the same set of goods. Will use EU comparison and controls for pre-shock import growth.

A3. Stable unit treatment value / no spillovers across industries.  
Plausibility: Some upstream–downstream linkages exist; we will add input-output controls and later examine propagation separately.

A4. Anticipation negligible before 2000.  
Plausibility: PNTR passed unexpectedly in Oct-2000 after contentious votes. We will include 1999–2000 leads to test.

A5. Consistent measurement and balanced panel.  
Plausibility: Census and Comtrade data are reliable; we will check for sample attrition.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Main Threats and Mitigation
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
T1. Differential pre-trends.  
• Event-study leads; falsification tests with 1980-1990s window.  
• Weighting by 1997 employment to avoid composition changes.

T2. Other China shocks (e.g., productivity, exchange-rate) that vary by product line.  
• Triple-difference with EU.  
• Instrument imports with NTRgap to show first-stage effect is PNTR-driven.

T3. Input-output spillovers (downstream users of Chinese inputs benefit, upstream compete).  
• Include Bartik-style downstream exposure controls.  
• Cluster s.e. by 2-digit sector to allow correlated shocks.

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
5. R Code Outline
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
```r
# ------------------ 0. Packages ------------------
library(data.table)
library(fixest)
library(ggplot2)
# ------------------ 1. Load data ------------------
usa <- fread("us_industry_panel.csv")       # must contain id, year, employ, ntr, non_ntr, imports, etc.
eu  <- fread("eu_industry_panel.csv")

# Harmonise industry codes
common_cols <- intersect(names(usa), names(eu))
panel <- rbindlist(list(usa[, ..common_cols][, country := "US"],
                        eu [, ..common_cols][, country := "EU"]))

# ------------------ 2. Variable construction ------------------
panel[, NTRgap := non_ntr_tariff - ntr_tariff]        # in percentage points
panel[, HighGap := as.integer(NTRgap >= median(NTRgap)), by = country] 
panel[, Post := as.integer(year >= 2001)]             # robustness: 2002
panel[, US := as.integer(country == "US")]

# Event-time dummies for ±7 years
for(k in -7:8){
  panel[, paste0("tau",k) := as.integer(year - 2001 == k)]
}

# ------------------ 3. Baseline DID (US only) ------------------
us_only <- panel[country=="US"]
est1 <- feols(log(employment) ~ Post*NTRgap | industry + year,
              data = us_only, cluster = ~industry)
summary(est1)

# ------------------ 4. Triple-difference ------------------
est2 <- feols(log(employment) ~ US*Post*NTRgap | industry + country.year,
              data = panel, cluster = ~industry)
summary(est2)

# ------------------ 5. Event-study ------------------
lags <- paste0("tau", -6:-1)
leads <- paste0("tau",0:6)
formula_es <- as.formula(
  paste("log(employment) ~", 
        paste(c(lags, leads), collapse="+"), "*NTRgap | industry + year"))
est_es <- feols(formula_es, data=us_only, cluster=~industry)
iplot(est_es, ref.line = 0)

# ------------------ 6. Robustness: placebo policy year 1995 ------------------
us_only[, PlaceboPost := as.integer(year >= 1995)]
placebo <- feols(log(employment) ~ PlaceboPost*NTRgap | industry + year,
                 data = us_only, cluster = ~industry)
summary(placebo)
```

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
6. Expected Results
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Theory predicts that removing tariff-uncertainty lowers domestic production in highly exposed industries by encouraging import expansion and importer entry.

Magnitude (industry level): A 10 p.p. larger NTR-gap is expected to reduce manufacturing employment by about 4–6 percent cumulatively over 2001-2007 (≈ 0.7–1 percent per year), consistent with calibrated trade elasticities of 3–4.

Other outcomes:  
• Imports from China: strong positive β (> 15 %).  
• Number of U.S. importing firms: positive.  
• Plant-level capital/labor ratio: rises (shift toward capital- or technology-intensive production in surviving plants).

----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1 = satisfied, 0 = doubtful)
----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
C1. Evidence of parallel pre-trends                        1  
C2. No simultaneous confounding policies                   0.5  
C3. No treatment mis-classification                        1  
C4. Limited spillovers/interference                        0.5  
C5. Correct inference & clustered s.e.                     1  

Total = 4/5 ⇒ reasonably credible, with residual concerns about spillovers and other China-specific shocks.
